speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. There appeared in this building this morning a delegation headed by the government of my province of Manitoba, with which were associated other organizations representing the citizens of my province. As a citizen of Manitoba and as a representative of hundreds of people affected by the matter concerning which this delegation came to Ottawa, I wished to associate myself with it, but I was barred from entry to the room where this delegation was making its presentation. In addition I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown), the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Teillet) and perhaps others were also barred. I protest against this action.
(Translation):

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES    REFUSAL OF PERMISSION TO ATTEND WITH DELEGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support that protest.
It seems to me that, in such a case, where an important delegation from Manitoba came here this morning and submitted a brief to the ministers of the crown, without the elected representatives of Manitoba being given the opportunity to be present and to assist that delegation, it is fitting that I join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in protesting against such an action.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ENTRY OF GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon.
members know, in so far as the Six are concerned the negotiations which have been going on in Paris since October, 1961 terminated today, at least for the time being. The latest information I have in that connection is that the five members other than France continued some discussion this afternoon following the conclusion of the negotiations among the Six. This naturally becomes a matter of very considerable moment to our country and to the countries of the free world as to what course should be adopted at this time.
The attitude taken by this government in regard to British entry was set out in the

statement which I made to the prime ministers' conference in September last, in which I stated:
We wish to emphasize first of all that the decision regarding the entry into E.E.C. is one for Britain and Britain alone, after the consultation which this meeting has made possible and such further consultation as may be desired.
The Canadian government is not taking a position on whether or not the U.K. should enter the common market because we respect the right of Britain to take this decision herself. We have been invited to tell the British government of our assessment of the effects of such a decision upon Canadian interests and we have done so. There are many other considerations involved in this decision which only the British government and the British parliament can take properly into account.
At that time I proposed that whatever the outcome of this conference might be, an invitation should be extended "to all member nations of the commonwealth, of the E.E.C., E.F.T.A., the United States of America and Japan and other like minded nations indicating a desire to participate, to meet at the earliest practicable date to give consideration to how to deal with the trading problems before us in a way which will be to the mutual advantage of all". Then I said this:
This should prepare the way for the prospective non-discriminatory tariff negotiations on a most favoured nation basis.
Then I pointed out the following:
I believe that this would offer a practical contribution to the solution of our difficulties which will advance the strength of commonwealth association, will permit the common market to proceed with the expansion of its own activities, and will bring to bear the immense trading capacity of the U.S.A. and Japan.
As the house knows, subsequently I brought this proposal to the attention of the President of the United States and it was accepted. I referred to that on October 16 last and some discussion took place at that time. In connection with this meeting suggested by me and accepted by the President of the United States, in which Canada and the United States joined, the council of GATT will be meeting in a few days for the purpose of deciding on the ministerial meeting. I think in view of what has taken place in Brussels today everything should be done to speed up the holding of the ministerial meeting so that these various like minded nations that I have named, together with the commonwealth countries, the European economic community, and the European free trade association can meet together.
As far as the commonwealth is concerned, today I had a conversation with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in this regard. Consultations I am sure will be continuing now among the various member
Inquiries of the Ministry nations of the commonwealth as to what would be the appropriate course to take within the commonwealth without in any way derogating from the ministerial meeting which, although it was generally agreed in the last few days that it could not take place before April 1, might be advanced to a considerably earlier date.
I hope to be in the United Kingdom on February 25, and at that time there will be an opportunity to consult with the British government on this matter, particularly with regard to the commonwealth. After all, as I said in September, the decision was for Britain. Britain has now, apparently, found it impossible at this time to join on terms that would have safeguarded to any degree the commonwealth relationship and commonwealth preferences. That being so, no time must be lost in bringing together, by consultation, the various parts of the commonwealth in order that full and informal discussions, to begin with, may take place without delay and also, at the same time, to do everything we can to expand multilateral trade in all parts of the world through the medium of discussions and conclusions reached at the ministerial meeting of GATT.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ENTRY OF GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has just made a statement on a matter of the greatest possible importance, and it is to be regretted that circumstances do not permit the kind of discussion of this subject which its importance, both immediate and ultimate, would justify.
The attitude of the opposition toward the negotiations which have been going on for months with a view to the United Kingdom joining the European common market has been clearly expressed, I believe, on many occasions. We on this side have from the beginning been sympathetic to this development, though agreeing with the Prime Minister that it is, of course, a matter for the decision of the United Kingdom alone. We were sympathetic, and we favoured this development if it could be brought about on suitable terms and under suitable conditions; because we on this side felt that the United Kingdom as a member of the European common market would help to ensure that the coming together of Europe both economically and politically would be brought about in a way which would not be inward looking or exclusive but so as to encourage the removal of obstructions between the new organization and the outside world. We thought British membership would have an important and desirable effect in the right direction.
We also supported the move because we thought it would be a further step in the
3208	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry development of the Atlantic community, and that based on this Atlantic community the best possible arrangements could be made with other countries in what we called the free world. It would appear there has been a setback to this development, a setback which even now, we must hope, will not be permanent. Any one member of the European community which accepts responsibility for keeping the United Kingdom outside of the European community is taking a heavy responsibility on itself.
When the Prime Minister said on Friday last, as reported on page 3126 of Hansard-
The agreement signed in Paris (between President de Gaulle and Dr. Adenauer) represents a forward step which would never have been contemplated ten years ago.
-I found myself at that time disagreeing with his analysis of that particular agreement. However, the information today is that there has been a serious setback. The Prime Minister has rightly said, what can we do now in the commonwealth and, indeed, in the free world to ensure that this setback is not a permanent one in its effect on bringing about better relations among all countries, not only in trade but in other ways. The Prime Minister has talked about the GATT ministerial meeting. That meeting is an essential process, more essential now, perhaps, than it was. It must be remembered that a preparatory committee in connection with this meeting was set up nearly a year ago. It is to be hoped that this preparatory work can be brought to a conclusion with the least possible delay.
The development made known today is bound to have an important effect on the United States trade expansion act because that act was predicated upon the United Kingdom becoming a member of the European common market. If the United Kingdom should now be kept out of that market, the President of the United States will have to amend in some respects the trade expansion program act passed by congress last year. It is to be hoped that this will give the Canadian government an opportunity to share in any changes which may have to be made to that act so that we may associate ourselves, even at this stage, with the United States in the negotiations which may be required, through GATT, with the European common market, even without the United Kingdom. Such negotiations however will have to include the United Kingdom and other members of the commonwealth as well.

I believe everyone of us in this house has watched with intense interest the development of the situation in Europe as it relates to the entry of Britain into the European common market.


We are concerned with the action which has been taken on the part of the president of France and by the apparent inability of the British negotiators to make their point with the European economic community council.
This is not the time to enter into a debate on this topic nor is it the time when we should be looking backward at things which might have happened or at things which might have been done. I believe it is our duty to evaluate the situation with regard to our own responsibilities and the part Canada herself can play in this situation.
This does not relate so much to Britain and her relationship with the E.E.C. or to the affairs of the other nations which compose that organization. It brings us back to the fact that we in the commonwealth have a definite responsibility. I think it would have been to our advantage had we, last fall, called for a commonwealth trade conference and moved forward with that project. I believe that at the present time the moment is opportune for such a move to be made. In fact it is urgent that Canada should take the lead in this regard. For too long we have stood back and waited to see what someone else proposed to do before we acted. We should be taking the lead now by calling the commonwealth together in a trade conference. We have an economic committee already set up which could do this work.
I believe we could do more to help Britain in her problem, as well as helping Canada, and I hope the government will take action along these lines as quickly as possible. We should, I believe, take a sympathetic attitude toward the problem which faces Britain, but it is about time we in Canada did something not only to help her but to help ourselves and to help the free association of nations which we now have in the commonwealth.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ENTRY OF GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
The rejection of the British application for membership in the European economic community will have far reaching repercussions for the United Kingdom and for the world, as well as for Canada as an important exporting nation.
On this day when there will be a good deal of disappointment in many quarters it should not be forgotten that when the treaty of Rome was signed in 1957 Britain could have entered the European common market without any difficulty whatsoever, and that she refused to do so rather than destroy the commonwealth preference system because she felt she had an obligation to the other members of the commonwealth. We should keep that in mind and remember that Britain made a serious sacrifice in order to preserve the commonwealth ties and to retain the commonwealth

preference system. Now that she has been rejected it should also not be forgotten that this rejection arises out of the fact that General de Gaulle has sought increasingly to direct the European economic community inward rather than outward in its outlook. This, in my opinion, will destroy the European common market, because I do not think this inward look is shared by the other members of the European common market.
The Prime Minister has said that we must now decide what we are going to do. This is not the proper time to debate the matter. However, I want to say very briefly that there are three things which ought to be done. First of all, we ought to be doing more to adjust the balance of trade between Canada and the United Kingdom. Some four or five years ago, when visiting the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister talked about transferring 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom, that this would solve the imbalance from which Canada and the United Kingdom both suffer. It is true that imports from the United Kingdom have increased, but exports have increased even more, so that today Great Britain continues to buy from us 50 per cent more than we buy from her. This is something which ought to be receiving the attention of the government and of this parliament.
The other matter is that I think the government ought to go back and see whether or not the United Kingdom is prepared to resubmit the proposal she made for a free trade agreement between Canada and Great Britain, that proposal which the government rejected out of hand in 1957. I think this could be extended to the entire commonwealth if the proper negotiations were proceeded with.
Third, I suggest that this is a time for the government to open negotiations with the United States to discuss the implications of the trade expansion act. The Prime Minister has spoken about the GATT ministerial conference. Such a conference will have merit, but surely anyone who is familiar with the problems of GATT will be aware of the fact that this is a long process of negotiation, and that the immediate hope lies first in helping to reduce the imbalance of our trade with Britain; second, in getting greater free trade within the commonwealth; and third, in entering into negotiations for freer trade with the United States under the provisions of the trade expansion act. If the European common market can be persuaded-which I doubt -by General de Gaulle to go it alone, then the commonwealth, the United States and the other parts of the world must make their trading arrangements accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last evening, I was saying that I agreed to the general principle of the bill now under consideration, and I was ex-

National Economic Development Board pressing the opinion that planning under the conditions now prevailing in the country, has become essential to the solution of our economic problems.
Yet, I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether the scheme, as it stands now, may become the efficient planning instrument that the government thinks it is putting at the disposal of our country's economy. The bill to set up the national economic development board is strangely similar to the bill which set up, in 1960, the national productivity council, and we might have grounds to fear that that new body will have a career as fruitless as that of the national productivity council.
The fact that only one of its advisers, that is to say the chairman himself, is called upon to work full time on this board, makes from the start the undertaking rather uncertain and problematical.
The bill also provides for the appointment of a maximum of 25 advisers, that is, the same number that was provided by the national productivity council. It would be quite surprising, Mr. Chairman, that such a large group of persons could produce anything but much discussion and little action. It would be preferable that the number of members be limited to three or five, perhaps, and that these work full time toward the achievement of the board's objectives.
I feel also that we should be concerned about the fact that there is no reference at all to the method of co-operation between the board itself and the government agencies. The bill setting up the national productivity council provided for the appointment of four officials from the departments concerned; this bill, however, does not provide for anything of the kind, and limits the relations between the board and the government to the reports which shall be made by the chairman to the Minister of Finance. In fact, the bill now under study does not confer any specific function, work or responsibility to the board; it merely instructs it to consider certain situations and report to the minister.
Besides, the bill itself recognizes implicitly that the members who will serve on that board without pay will effectively do little work since it provides, in a rather funny way, that members who perform duties in addition to their ordinary duties as members of the board, will receive a remuneration.
The general impression one gets from the bill is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) will have in hand a poor instrument to accomplish things otherwise quite praiseworthy.

Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the bill was prepared with too much haste and I find it hard to believe that an instrument so uncertain and indefinite could become, through the action of some voluntary advisers, a dynamic planning agency. If we were to appraise the bill in itself instead of accepting the interpretation given by the minister, there is a real danger that the national economic development board might be abandoned to its own resources; it will struggle along, begging interviews from the responsible ministers while being stuck with the suggestions it would like to have implemented.
If that planning project is really going to fill the present requirements, the national economic development board should be the very life and soul of the national economy. It should also be able to attend to the most pressing things first and to grapple with the immediate problems like chronic unemployment.
I think more particularly of the eastern Ontario region, which does not seem to have participated to the extent one might expect in the industrial development of the post-war years. It is not because resources are lacking, far from it. Manpower, skilled labour, excellent communications, plentiful hydroelectric resources, there is everything that could be required to bring about the economic growth of a whole area. No doubt the problem would not exist to the same extent had we agreed to give that region of the province a supply of the hydroelectric power developed to the benefit of other more fortunate regions of the province, at the price of great sacrifices that were required of the residents of that region. That decision did a great harm to all eastern Ontario and perhaps it would not have been reached if, at that time, there had been an agency like the national economic development board.
I am also thinking, Mr. Chairman, about the particular case of the area I represent in this house, and which is waiting with an increasing anxiety for the government to do something to put a stop to a situation that the most laudable efforts of the local authorities have never been able to correct.
I regret to recall here that, according to the latest official reports, more than 2,500 applicants for unemployment insurance benefits were registered with the commission's office, in Cornwall. It is an increase-seasonal perhaps but still an increase-of 700, as compared to the end of November. On the other hand, more than 3,200 persons are

National Economic Development Board
registered as seeking jobs, that is an increase of 600 over the previous month. Those figures do not substantially differ from what they were these last years; they illustrate how chronic the unemployment plague has become in this country.
I will not tax the patience of the committee by recalling in detail all the initiatives taken in that particular area to solve locally, through the only facilities at the disposal of a municipality, the economic problems of that community. Similar laudable efforts have been made in other areas, and that resourcefulness redounds to the credit of our municipalities. If enthusiasm, good will and initiative could by themselves bring in new industries, increase salaries and create employment, municipalities which, like Cornwall, have left no stone unturned to get rid by themselves of their economic plight would all benefit today from full prosperity and employment.
Unfortunately, the increasingly sharp competition between provinces, between various areas and between municipalities, in regard to the acquisition of new industrial enterprises, too often results in cancelling out particular efforts and in rendering fruitless local initiatives. Since economic problems continue to exist, in spite of all the hard work done by municipalities, it becomes imperative to look for solutions to those problems at higher levels of government.
We believe, Mr. Chairman, that the government must rethink the whole economic pattern of this country. I do not think this government has now a clear, precise, logical and long term plan to steer the economy of this country in a way that will solve the greatest problem today, chronic regional unemployment.
The setting up of the national economic development board is a step, faltering and long overdue no doubt, but still a step in the right direction. The planning of our economy could be of great help to us. But some people think that such planning should not be too easily entrusted to so many councils, committees and commissions, which the government is setting up with a generous enthusiasm.
The gradual surrendering of the ministers' prerogatives to commissioners and advisers is leading us toward the establishment of a technocracy which is contrary to democratic principles. It would have been much easier to support the bill under discussion if the minister had brought before the house a positive and detailed policy of economic planning of 27507-3-204
his own, for which he would have assumed responsibility and whose application would have been under his direct supervision. The alternate proposal submitted to us is a plan to find a plan. And if the search is successful, as we all hope, it will not be the work of the government, but rather of its technical advisors. Who knows if it will not be necessary later on to appoint a new board to carry out the recommendations of the national economic development board?
As I said earlier, Mr. Chairman, this bill is a step in the right direction, as long as other measures will supplement it without delay in order to make possible a fair and orderly development in all parts of the country.

Mr. Chairman, the aim of economic activities has always been to produce as much as possible with the least effort possible. Automation should please man, should help him, should exalt him in his country, instead of pushing him in that kind of insecurity which demoralizes him.
Why does the state exist? To lead or to serve? We must realize where the duty of the state lies. What is the purpose of this bill to set up a national economic development board? What is it about? Production activities? Processing operations? Manufactures? Plants? Increase production? Agriculture? Transport?
I wonder what is the aim of all those activities. Why do they exist? Of course, their raison d'etre is to meet the needs of human beings. That is the aim of any sound economy; to fill the need for appropriate goods and profits. Production and industry therefore exist to serve.
Furthermore, we are convinced that with modern means of production and transport, it is possible and relatively easy to put enough goods at the disposal of all consumers to satisfy all their essential needs. If that result is not achieved, the fault does not lie with production itself, and it does not lie either with the will of the consumers.
Since the aim of production is to meet the needs of consumers, it follows that consumers must have the means to make their needs known to production; it is to the master to make his desires known to his servant.
We have here a bill concerning economic development, under which the government will be authorized to direct; and thanks to that power, even if the people are in need of 27507-3-204J
National Economic Development Board bread, the government will be able to say that it is guns that are needed-exactly what the people do not want.
Reference is made in this bill to planned or directed economy. To direct means to draw, to push in a given direction. In what direction? If it is not directed in the direction of its final objective, it will go astray; and if its final objective consists in meeting the needs of consumers, is it not consumers themselves?
Yet, is that really the idea entertained by those who are requesting a planned economy? Are they not thinking rather in terms of an economy in which the government will put its finger in all control institutions and will tell production what to do and consumers what they must accept?
If that is the kind of direction which is requested, let us realize at once that we already have, and that we have had for several decades, a directed economy. It is directed by those who are in a position to give orders to production, by those who are in a position to dictate their conditions to producers, and by no stretch of the imagination could we say that it is the people, with their needs, who are giving orders to production.
Who suffers from hunger? Members of families where there are more mouths to feed than there is money in the pocketbook. Are they the ones who give orders to food producers?
Who suffers from cold, sickness and the lack of clothing? Are they the ones who give orders to suppliers of firewood and fuel oil, to clothing manufacturers, doctors and druggists?
Who is most in need? Those who live in plain houses. Is it for them that thousands of people work in our industrial cities? Who gets the carloads of commodities which come out of our manufactures?
Production is diverted from its end. Shoes are produced not for the comfort of the people but to enrich the manufacturers. Thousands of people go barefoot while thousands of pairs of shoes remain in storage and on store shelves. Incentives are being sought for production without any thought being given to the consumers.
Indeed, that condition is imposed at the very source where the money required for production comes from. It is the manufacturer who borrows money and the banker who lends it who decide to what use the money will be put. That is where decisions are made concerning the proposed production and where authorization to speed up or slow down production comes from. The banker's book is
3220	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board supreme; absolutely no consideration is given to the consumers' needs. What is the use of planning?
Everybody knows that today's overabundant production has not met the enormous needs of the world and it is on this most revolting historical fact, that those who promote a planned economy base themselves.
But it is noteworthy that most of the laws that advocate a planned economy are very careful not to make the slightest reference to the power that is directing the economy at the present time. They recognize that the economy is not directed towards the needs of the consumers, but they merely ask the government to intervene to give orders to producers.
We forget that the government itself takes orders from an outside power since it takes so few measures for the good of all. Being itself under the power of money "barons", how can the government intervene except under orders and under pressure from those money "barons"? The government should get its freedom back first.
But once that has been achieved, should it behoove the government to state the needs of the consumers? Is not its function rather to remove the obstacles so that the consumers themselves can make their needs known?
There is a very simple way for the consumers to make their needs known to production and the first duty of a government worthy of that name should be to offer it to the consumers. That is the only guidance, the only logical intervention needed.
Put some familiar looking pieces of paper in each consumer's pocket, or give him only an account on which to draw cheques, and you will see if each consumer will not start at once to place orders with production; and if that situation is allowed to remain unchanged, production will automatically meet the needs of the consumers.
Money is like a right to vote with regard to products. If production exists for the consumers, that right to vote must be given to the consumers. The dollar is the voting slip through which the consumer chooses the product that suits him. Therefore, it is with this voting slip that the consumer will direct the industry, finance through his purchases the enterprise that works for him and eliminate by refusing it his slip, the one which pursues other aims.
Production is very efficient provided it is left alone. Let us take the case of the shoe-


making industry; a woman buys three pairs of shoes for the members of her family. You never hear the owner of the store say that he cannot let these three pairs of shoes go lest he might not be able to replace them. The manufacturer is only waiting for the order to supply more, and the owner of the store knows it.
Shoes are being replaced with the same unfailing certainty as a cause produces its effects.
But apply a regulation that will take away from the woman the possibility of buying the shoes; then production will slow down in proportion; for example, if the husband does not work, there is no salary coming in, and on the basis of the reward and punishment system which has taken over the field of economy, being out of work, he has therefore no right to production. The right to production is reserved as a reward; the man having not earned that reward, the shoes will stay there and the members of the family will go bare feet.
The manufacturer will not provide shoes of all sizes, not that he is not able to do so, but on account of a rule that stands against it. Production will automatically supply consumers as long as the latter are able to voice their needs to production and unless interference is exercised by a power beyond both the producer and the consumer.
However, through a philosophy that bears the strong stamp of Judaism, the pursuit of an end pertaining to morals is inflicted upon economy. Industry and production are being made a management implement instead of a service implement. Industry thus finds itself in a cramped position; it is being asked to do something that does not come within its functions and is prevented from achieving its end.
Its own end directs it to supply as many useful things as possible with the least possible effort; and the nearer it gets to it, the more it is crippled by the rule of reward and punishment. The man who is not called upon to produce must not enjoy the fruits of production.
The more industry improves, the more it eliminates human labour and the authorized consumer. And, always on account of the system of reward and punishment, the more it suppresses the authorized consumer, the more it is condemning itself to stagnation, unless it is directed towards activities having to do with destruction, as is the case today; warfare is the salvation of the system.
The conditioning of the right to the necessary things of life has become such an instrument of management that it is being used

National Economic Development Board
unconsciously by those who want to manage others and who have neither the virtue nor the efficiency to succeed otherwise.
This is the axis around which political patronage, intimidation and economical dicta-ture, at all levels, are rotating.
It is the hidden government of money interests, the government of those who, being absolute masters of money and of credit, distribute them according to their fancies and control even our right to breathe.
When the Social Crediters ask for a bare minimum for everybody, through the payment of a national dividend, regardless of any personal contribution to production, do we not find our opponents always eager to mention the moral danger involved? If, all of a sudden, man could feed himself without having to toil, what a catastrophe that would be and how could he be kept under the yoke.
And yet, the economy is not meant to govern, but to serve. Its concern is to supply the earthly goods man must have to meet his temporal needs; its moral character is to be found in the achievement of that goal, not in substituting it to morals.
It is to mystify the multitude and to prevent or delay the true reforms that the profiteers of our present financial system take cover behind moral considerations, the moment that means are sought to put an end to their deadly swindles.
If the plans set forth here and there favour regimentation-statements made by prominent people have more or less as their common denominator regimentation, state employment, state enterprise, control for the centralization of power, the loss of national sovereignties, and, it goes without saying, provincial sovereignties and individual freedom-it is precisely because preparations are being made to deal with current problems without disturbing the present financial set-up.
It is found that, with the financial system we now have, there is no other alternative to the economic slump than socialism, avowed or not. And, because the financial set-up is not to be tampered with, the way is being paved for socialism; instead of having the financial system conform to the needs of humanity, it is humanity that has to conform to the requirements of the financial system.
The Social Crediters are the only ones who have the courage to attack the financial system, and for that we are found guilty of a crime. Each time we make some progress, a pack of people rise against us and, in this pack, it is surprising to find forces and men
who, taking their responsibilities, denounce socialism.
We are the only ones to fight for the respect of free enterprise, for the respect of the human being, and for the idea that each man should receive the bare minimum required for a decent livelihood, for the achievement of a life really worth living, in security and in peace.
Mr. Chairman, the only alternative that we bring in, in order to improve our economy, is to lay down plans and more plans. People are tired of all those plans which mean nothing. This bill concerning the establishment of a national economic development board will not bring money into the pockets of our citizens: they will keep on starving. Fifty years may go by before anything comes out of this bill, if anything ever comes out of it.
We may be all dead before any results from this disastrous economic bill start showing.
We are opposed to this economic bill. We are in favour of a system which will bring life and not death. People want to live with dignity; they want to see their legal, moral and social rights fully respected. That is the reason why we are fighting. We Social Crediters, demand the right for each individual, everything which is available: the right to production, the right to modernization, the right to everything his forefathers have achieved before him. We are here to demand those rights and we do so with all our strength.

National Economic Development Board whether it is possible or desirable under this bill to have that kind of an inquiry. I am not certain in my own mind whether it is possible under the bill to establish a committee or a body, to provide for the remuneration of the people involved and to give them terms of reference that would enable them to do a comprehensive job. I want to tell the Minister of Finance that the people on the prairies who are particularly concerned with this whole problem of rail line abandonment are absolutely opposed to the board of transport commissioners being given the job. They feel that basically the board of transport commissioners is a court of record. They feel that it is involved with detailed consideration of railway questions such as freight rates, and that any general study of the economic services provided by branch lines and the adverse effect of their removal should be undertaken by a board or body outside of and apart from the board of transport commissioners.
While the question of rail line abandonment has been raised in the three prairie provinces mainly, I believe the Minister of Finance would agree with me when I say that this whole problem is likely to have a very important and very serious impact on the maritime provinces. Therefore, while it is a problem that today is being focused on the prairies, mainly because of the aggressive action of farm leaders and organizations in that part of the country, it is nevertheless something that has a very broad scope. I would ask the minister whether it would be possible in his opinion, under the terms of the bill as they now exist, to set up a committee or body that would have representation from the railways, the federal government, the provinces and the organizations which have been particularly involved, to study the serious economic effect and the serious cost to communities of a large scale abandonment of railway services and to look into, amongst other things, the efficiency or inefficiency of the operations of the railway companies having to do with branch line services.
I can tell the committee there have been brought to my attention a great many accusations that the railway companies are deliberately operating branch line services in such a way as to show large losses. The belief of the people making these statements is that these losses are being incurred so as to bolster the arguments of the companies at a later date in their applications to abandon lines. Here are some examples of what I have been told: sending in special trains to pick up goods when the regular biweekly schedule would do; discontinuing a passenger service and, on the very day it is discon-

tinued, laying down tile in the waiting room the passengers used to use; saving an expenditure of $6 in wages with the result that a special train has to be sent in at a cost of $800.
I realize this has been a broad and far-ranging discussion. We had a long discourse on Social Credit theory a while ago. But I think it is very pertinent to this bill to inquire whether or not such an important question as the discontinuance of branch line services is the kind of thing which could be inquired into under this measure. I am not asking the minister whether this bill is to be used as a vehicle for such an inquiry or not. I do not expect to get that information from him. But I wonder if he would comment on his understanding of the general terms of this legislation and tell us whether a committee of inquiry of a type which would be as independent and as competent as the chairman whom the minister wishes to appoint could be set up to inquire into this whole question and, by so doing, meet the demands of so many organizations that an impartial and independent inquiry be undertaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member has asked a pertinent question. I am not going to give any categorical answer at the moment, but he knows that the powers set forth in clauses 9, 10, 11 and 12 are very wide. These provisions would, I think, give this board the power to investigate any problem relevant to the development of the economy of the nation. So I think I can say affirmatively that this board would have the power to conduct inquiries into this matter.
It should also be borne in mind that the intention of the government and, I am sure, of this committee in setting up the board is to deal with long term problems and I understand that the problem which the hon. member has raised is, at least in some areas, of a short term nature because the impact will be felt in the relatively near future if something is not done in connection with it. As the hon. member knows, the bill which deals with this matter is being held up at the moment until the premiers from the three western provinces come here next week. I may also say-and I do not think this has been said before-that this problem is not one limited exclusively to the prairie provinces. It has its impact directly on other provinces in Canada, and I may say, in passing, that the premier of Nova Scotia is coming here some time early next week-* he has asked for an appointment on Tuesday or Wednesday-to discuss with the government the very question which has been raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia. So, with-

out saying that this bill would constitute the ideal machinery to deal with this problem I would say affirmatively that this question could be dealt with by the board if that were the desire of the house or the government at any time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I thank the minister for his answer. I would simply say that I welcome the information that the premier of Nova Scotia will be in Ottawa to discuss the important question of railway branch lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I can qualify that. He is coming to discuss not only the problem of branch lines but also other problems in the field of transportation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
No doubt he will be discussing other matters, too. We can think of all kinds of questions he might discuss.
I was about to say it is somewhat difficult for those of us who come from the prairies when we are made aware of a belief on the part of some people that this is purely a prairie question. It is a national question and I am sure it will be raised on a national basis just as soon as there are applications for the removal of branch lines in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces to the degree that these applications have been forthcoming on the prairies. It is clear, however, from the evidence, that the prairies have had to take the lead in trying to get the government, after months of delay, to do something about these continuing applications to remove branch lines. The minister has said this is a short run affair. Well, if your railway is to be taken from you, you can call it short run or long run. If it is taken from you the day after tomorrow, I suppose it is a short run action but the difficulties and inconveniences will last as long as you live, or as long as you reside in that community. I would remind the minister, because he knows, already, that the MacPherson commission recommendation on this point has to do with the removal of branch line services over a period of 15 years. Here is a question, obviously, which requires long term planning and long term action. If this is to be merely short term action on the basis of the balance sheets of the railway companies, I ask the government what possible economic advantage would it be to the country to remove branch line services if by doing so you save the railway companies $1 and cost the communities involved something in excess of a dollar in increased costs? This is an important question and I am not certain what should be done about it, not having, as yet, seen the legislation which the government is to bring down to deal specifically with this problem. However, it is because of the determined opposition in western Canada to this job being
National Economic Development Board given to the board of transport commissioners that I thought it worth while putting my inquiry to the minister. I thank him for his opinion that there is sufficient scope under this legislation to enable the kind of general inquiry I have in mind to be undertaken.

speechtext:
During the general
discussion mention has been made of the planning programs of various European countries including the United Kingdom. Mention has been made that the chancellor of the exchequer, who holds a position in the United Kingdom similar to that occupied by the minister of finance here, occupies the post of chairman of the Neddy council. Can the minister say whether or not any consideration has been given to this arrangement and what his feeling in connection with the proposal is. It will be remembered that my hon. friend from Coast-Capilano emphasized this in his speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I should say, I suppose, that this is a suggestion to which consideration was given in the preliminary drafting of the bill. The official with whom I was associated realized that in the United Kingdom the chancellor of the exchequer was the chairman of a board popularly called Neddy. I would not say that we gave too careful consideration to this because it was felt that it was unusual on a board such as this, one to which we wanted to attract all areas of our economy to give advice to the government. It was felt that there might be some difficulty in appointing a member of the executive for the time being, whatever might be the party in power, or whoever he might be, to be chairman of the board. It was felt that the board should be kept relatively small, as has been pointed out by various hon. members; that there should be a permanent chairman who would give direction to the operations of the board and who would not be responsible for administrative details or responsibilities, as would a minister. I know that I do not have to remind the hon. member for Essex East of the problems of a minister in any department. Although it is true-and I say this without any reflection upon Neddy-that the chancellor of the exchequer in the United Kingdom is the chairman of the board, he carries so many responsibilities that I am quite sure he does not give the intensive direction to that board which we felt a chairman should give to this one. Therefore, it was decided by the government, and I suggest properly decided, that the chairman should be somebody brought in from outside who would act as chairman of the board, in the same way that other government

National Economic Development Board boards have chairmen outside of the executive.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister's statement is an important one. It clearly indicates that the government does not have in mind the kind of body which exists in the United Kingdom, which exists in France, and about which we had some considerable detail from the hon. member for Gaspe yesterday in the very excellent speech which he delivered. We have no indication from the government of any intention to have a liaison between the government as such and this board except, as will be found in subsequent provisions in the bill, occasion is offered for reporting by the board to the minister. We will not even have what they have in France, the existence of a government rapporteur, who sits not only in the councils which have to do with the public, as well as the private sector. In France, in the top council, the "conseil superieur" and in the "commissariat du plan", provision is made for the existence of a rapporteur who represents the government. This we are not to have in the case of this particular board being set up by this bill. This gives an indication at this stage in our proceedings that the government does not have in mind the kind of planning body which the national productivity council special mission to Europe has reported on so favourably and which it has recommended for adoption in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into a discussion on the details with the hon. member. As I said last night, the constitutional situation in France and in the United Kingdom, and in other European countries as well, is quite different from that in this country where we have a federal state, with provinces, and where the laws are such that it is very difficult to set up a unitary commission such as you might have in France or in other countries. Also in this country, rightly or wrongly, and I am sure the hon. member for Essex East will agree with me rightly, the state does not have the degree of control over industry which it has, shall we say, for instance, in France; so I suggest there is no complete parallel which one can draw between the two. When we come to the consideration of clauses 9, 10 and 11 we find that the duties and responsibilities of the board are set out. In clause 12 it is provided that:
The board shall, to the greatest possible extent consistent with the performance of its duties under this act, co-operate with the national productivity council, the Atlantic development board, and all departments, branches and other agencies of the government of Canada-
I can assure the hon. member that it is the intent of those who are responsible for


the inception, the drafting and the presentation of this bill to parliament that the closest co-operation and liaison between this board and all other facets of the Canadian economy, so far as the federal government is concerned, will take place, and I hope that that is also the case with the provincial governments in so far as they feel they can co-operate with this board in the development of the Canadian economy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not want the remarks of the minister to be construed as establishing that we on this side had recommended overlooking the federal character of our constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, I did not mean that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure the minister did not mean that. But because he has made the observation, I think some comment is essential. I clearly indicated when speaking on the resolution that a complete parallel between what we proposed and what exists in various European nations was not possible in Canada because in every instance we were dealing with unitary states in Europe, whereas in Canada we have a federal state with ten provincial bodies operating and exercising sovereign powers under section 92 of the British North America Act. This difference between our constitutional set-up and that of the European countries offers in itself no justification, it seems to me for the suggestion made by the minister. As I pointed out, or endeavoured to point out, in my previous statement, there must be the closest possible co-operation between the federal and provincial governments to make effective the purposes of a planning board which is intended to deal in a total way with the economic problems of Canada. Indeed, I complained that this bill was deficient, as we shall later show when we come to the pertinent clause, in that it does not make provision for the co-operation which must prevail between the two senior levels of government. The minister is quite right that because of the property and civil rights clause in the British North America Act, it is open only to the provinces to exercise those powers which are exercised, for instance, in the United Kingdom under the town and country planning act. But it should be possible, having in mind the fiscal powers of the federal government with regard to its general and unlimited tax policy, for the federal government to be able to work out arrangements in connection with the provincial power over industry, let us say, in any given province in order to meet the problem of, for example, the relocation of industry mentioned by the hon. member for Essex West the other evening. This bill will be one

National Economic Development Board
having a most limited scope unless we provide in it an obligation of the board and of the government to bring about a co-operative effort between the two levels of government to achieve objectives which we think even in a limited way are encompassed in clause 9 of the bill.
Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Establishment of board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to address a few remarks to the minister with respect to clause 3. We find this clause objectionable because there is no reference made to any action which the minister or the government must take with regard to consulting any of the principal organizations throughout the country which represent the various economic areas of Canadian life, presumably the very organizations the co-operation and assistance of which are going to be required if the aims of this board are to be realized. I think an outstanding example of the very thing which could happen here and which happened to a board somewhat similar in function to this one, namely the national productivity council, was the resignation of Mr. Claude Jodoin. It is not so much an example of the fact that he represents the Canadian Labour Congress but of the fact that he represents a large organization and presumably speaks for a large number of people in one specific area of our economic life. This could apply to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association or any other such organization where the government wishes to appoint a representative of that organization and puts men on a board, but owing to dissatisfaction with the manner of the appointment it did not get the co-operation of the association involved.
In pointing out the example of the appointment of Mr. Claude Jodoin, I would say that he resigned from the national productivity council on the basis that he was appointed without being consulted prior to his appointment. That is the first point. The second point is that he was not appointed as a representative of the large organization of which he was the head, namely the Canadian Labour Congress, and therefore felt that any contribution he could make to the national productivity council was severely limited, in that he could not speak for the Canadian Labour Congress, the very congress whose co-operation the national productivity council needed ever so badly, since the co-operation of labour and management was an essential to any proper carrying out of the duties of the national productivity council.
I cannot see how this legislation prevents a similar occurrence taking place with respect
to the national economic development board. Again, and I may say this matter has been gone into several times in this House of Commons, the duties of this board seem to overlap to a considerable extent those of the national productivity council. Perhaps it is the suspicion of many of us that the ultimate purpose is to have it take over the national productivity council. If that is so, it is all the more important that the manner of appointment is such as to ensure the utmost cooperation of management and labour, to say nothing of agriculture, or the purpose of the national economic board will never be realized.
In view of this consideration I think it is essential to make an amendment to this particular clause. At the same time this amendment, it will be noted, does not derogate from the government's ultimate responsibility and jurisdiction in making an appointment. What the amendment does is to ensure that the organizations whose assistance is essential for this body are consulted prior to the appointment and that to some degree the government can be assured that, once the appointment is made, the particular appointee will be able to commit to a considerable extent the principal organizations of the country of which he is a member to assist in the carrying out of this board's duties. To that end I should like to make the following amendment:
That the period in line 15 he replaced by a comma and the following words be added:
after consultation with the principal organizations representative of trade unions, farmers, and other groups as the governor in council may determine.

speechtext:
While we agree that some consideration should be given to this amendment, I believe it does not go nearly far enough. One of the problems in connection with the operation of the productivity council is that we are asking for advice and assistance from a number of groups and yet we are not allowing these groups to have an active part in the selection of their representatives, and therefore not after consultation with the governor in council but with the organizations which are interested in and concerned with this matter. They should have the opportunity of nominating their own representatives. The reason for this is simple. If we are going to ask for the co-operation of certain industries and certain large corporations as was done during the last war, then there is one thing that should be done. On that occasion we gave them representation in the form of dollar-a-year men in many cases. However, these men had the backing of the independent companies who were paying them, and they went

Private Bills
to their assignments with the understanding that if they made a suggestion to the government, that suggestion was one which they could put into effect.
While I do not wish to discuss the representatives of corporations, I know that in a union it is extremely difficult to elect, through convention or in any manner through which a representative may be chosen, one who will go and take part in deliberations in a council or other body and who is not in a position to commit the organization he is representing. This situation cannot come by selection. It cannot come by the governor in council asking for this, as actually that is the cabinet. It can come only if the representative is one who has the permission and direction of his organization to back up the representations he makes. I suggest that is something that has been done in days gone by and that in this particular case anything less will not be particularly successful. May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

maintopic: THE EVANGELICAL LUTHERAN SYNOD OF WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, as set out in the explanatory notes, is to give effect to an agreement of consolidation, effective as of July 1, 1962, whereby four large branches of the Lutheran church in the United States and Canada, namely American Evangelical Lutheran Church, the Augustana Evangelical Lutheran Church, the Finnish Evangelical Lutheran Church of America and the United Lutheran Church in America agreed to consolidate under the name of "Lutheran Church in America". The Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Western Canada was one of the synods of the United Lutheran Church in America.
The territorial jurisdiction of the Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Western Canada included the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and that part of Ontario lying west of the 86th meridian of longitude, the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories.
Under the terms of consolidation, this synod is to be known as central Canada synod of the Lutheran church in America and the territorial jurisdiction is to be limited to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba and that portion of the province of Ontario lying west of the 88th meridian of longitude.
Clause 1 of the bill changes the name of the corporation in accordance with the agreement of consolidation.
Clause 2 of the bill provides for the adherence of the corporation to the Lutheran church in America in ecclesiastical matters.

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. SD-6, for the relief of Sonja Bagry-Mr. Mandziuk -Mr. Paul in the chair.

On clause 1.

In so far as the bill before us is concerned, I have taken the liberty in the last few minutes of looking at the evidence upon which the bill is founded. There are a number of strange things about it which I think should be examined very closely by committee of the whole before the committee decides to recommend the bill to the house. I would particularly draw your attention to a few changes which were made in the petition as it was originally drafted and as it now appears in printed form before us. These changes took place before the committee of the Senate, and some of them make one wonder what the Senate committee was thinking about or trying to do when it made these changes.
In the first instance, part 1 of the petition upon which this bill is founded reads:
That on or about the 8th of May, 1945, your petitioner was lawfully married to the said-
Then, there is the name of the respondent.
-in Braunschweig, Germany.
However, in the evidence which was given before the committee by the petitioner, from which I should like to read a few excerpts, with the committee keeping in mind that the petition which is now printed before us contains the note that on or about the 8 May 1945, the marriage took place, different statements are made. The petitioner appeared, was sworn and proceeded to give certain evidence to which I must refer now. She identified herself, her address, occupation, religion and where she was married. Then, these questions were asked by the clerk of the committee:
Q. When were you married?
A. July 26, 1945.
There was no hesitation, just a direct statement, July 26, 1945. You will recall the petition as it is now printed gives the date as May 8, 1945. Then, the clerk says:
Q. I show you a document. Do you recognize this document?
A. Yes.

A. Yes.
Q. Have you seen this document before?

A. Yes.
Then, the marriage certificate was filed as exhibit 1. There are some other questions about recognizing a photograph of her husband and then the lawyer, Mr. Masse, asks these questions:

You had better amend the petition.
Then, the committee approves an amendment to the petition showing the date which appears on the marriage certificate. Let us remember that it took a series of questions by the clerk of the committee, by the lawyer representing her and by the chairman to get information as to the exact date of the marriage, and the answers ranged over two different months and two different dates in one month. Perhaps this is not important in itself, but it is important I think when we connect it with the other alterations and changes which were made in the petition and the other inconsistencies in the evidence given by those who appeared as witnesses.
There was another change which took place in the petition as it was originally presented and as it now appears before us. This was in clause No. 6 of the petition which now reads:
That after the said marriage and until the month of June, 1951, your petitioner lived and cohabited with the said-in Braunschweig, Germany to the month of November, 1947, and thereafter in Montreal, Canada, and that two children were born of the said marriage-
Then, the petition gives their names and the dates of their birth. In the petition as originally presented it indicated that there was only one child born of the marriage. Subsequent evidence brought to light the fact that there were two, one of whom had died, I believe in 1953. Accordingly, the petition was amended to cite the facts as they were, correctly.
That particular clause 6 of the petition also says that they came here to Canada in November, 1947 from Germany, and in the evidence which is given later on as to what time it was that they came here, the petitioner was not quite sure when it was and had to be prompted somewhat by the lawyer with respect to that particular time, but that was subsequently cleared up.
There is one other change in the petition which I submit is of great importance and should be studied at some length by this committee. It concerns clause 7 which I gather is the one of main substance, namely

Divorce Bills
that which alleges the commission of adultery. As it is printed the petition reads as follows:
That during the month of January, 1961 and on numerous other occasions in 1961 the said... committed adultery with one .. . housewife, residing at-
Further on it alleges that they were living, residing, cohabitating at that address as man and wife, or what is loosely referred to as a common law relationship. The particular point with which we must concern ourselves is that during the month of June, 1961, adultery was committed.
The committee must remember that petitions are not hastily drawn up. A petition is prepared by a lawyer who undoubtedly acquaints himself as fully as possible with all the facts to make sure everything is correct in the petition so far as its allegations are concerned. Now, the original petition reads: "That in the night of June 13th, 1961" certain things took place. That is subsequently changed by the committee of the other place to read "during the month of June, 1961". Instead of confining it to one evening or one day they expanded it to embrace the entire month of June.
I submit that was done for a particular purpose by the senators on the committee in the other place, namely, to bend over backwards if necessary to ensure that the allegations of adultery were proven, because if June 13 had remained in the petition, as will be shown later on, none of the three witnesses who appeared on behalf of the petitioner had any knowledge of what happened on the night of June 13 when it was originally alleged adultery took place. I say that the senators in the other place, in their overzealous desire for proper court procedures, expanded this period to give the benefit to the petitioner.
It was more than you are doing.

In answer to my hon. friend who interjects, all he has to do is communicate with the Prime Minister to try to inject some backbone into the Prime Minister, and perhaps then we will get some solution to this particular problem.
One of the witnesses called was a Joseph Szabo who, having been sworn, testified as to his name and his age being 33, his place of living being Montreal and his occupation being a cutter. He is not, as has been the case in many instances, a private investigator or detective, but an ordinary citizen following an ordinary course of activity. He is shown a photograph of the respondent. He recognizes the portrait and identifies it as the respondent, or husband in this particular case. Then certain questions are asked of him as follows:

Q. Do you know where he lives?
A. X know.
Q. What is his address?
He gives the address as it was contained in the petition.
Q. Do you know how long he has been living there, or since when do you know he has been living there?
A. I know since 1960, August.
Q. How do you know he is living there?
A. I was boarding there.
Here is an individual who lived as a boarder, I suppose for about a year, in a particular house where this respondent is alleged to have committed adultery.
Q. Was Mr. Bagry living alone in that dwelling?
A. No, he wasn't. He was living with his wife.
Q. With his wife?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know his wife? Can you show to us who his wife is?
A. Yes, this person here.
Obviously he pointed to somebody in the committee room. Then it continues:
By the Chairman:
Q. You are pointing to the corespondent?
A. Yes.
Q. I show you the petitioner in this case. That is not the woman you mean, is it?
A. No, I never saw her (the petitioner) in my life.
The same question is asked again and then another question:
Q. Do you know the other woman as the wife of Mr. Bagry?
A. Yes.
This indicates, on the evidence of this gentleman, who was a boarder at this residence, that for the period of time he was a boarder there until at least the time when the petition was presented-that would be from August, 1960 until June, 1961-the respondent and corespondent were living together as man and wife and presumably the corespondent was using the surname of the respondent, as one would think would happen. Apparently the lawyer did not think so because he proceeded to ask further questions. Q. Are there any children living that house? A. One girl.
Q. How old is she? A. Five or six; I don't know.

To which Mr. Masse replies:

took place on the night of June 13. A. No.

By the Chairman:
Q. I suppose he buys groceries from you?
A. Yes, but they take it themselves up. I may have been up once a long time ago at the beginning.
In so far as any knowledge on the part of this grocer is concerned with regard to adultery having taken place, he has not the foggiest idea. All he knows is that there is a couple living next door "upstairs some place" who take groceries upstairs. He has no knowledge of beds and the other accoutrements which go along with married life. He may have had some knowledge about the child, whether or not he thought her to be the child of this couple, but he gives no evidence about that. As far as the grocer is concerned we can completely discount his evidence as to adultery, unless we take it that he knew them together in the area for some seven years as one selling groceries to them. He said that they perhaps represented themselves as man and wife.
I suggest that this is what the committee in the other place did, and this is what was particularly in the mind of the chairman and the other members of the committee: they had convinced themselves early enough in the proceedings before that committee that there was a so-called common law relationship, and that was good enough for them. They were merely trying to get some little bit of information to prove adultery. That is why they persisted in inquiring about the night of June 13. We now find two witnesses have appeared, neither one of whom knows anything about the night of June 13 and the allegation that adultery was committed there. In each case when he was asked the lawyer representing the petitioner said: "No,

I am not going to prove this by either of these two witnesses; I have another witness coming".
Can I ask a question?
Certainly.
Is it true there are 492 private bills before us which have been accepted by the other place; and is it not your opinion that we should accept all of these bills together?

The answer to that question is simply no. In the first place, I have not much faith in the other place. Second, I have found out they have been misled before, because people who appeared before the committee of the other place have been sentenced to penitentiary terms for committing perjury in divorce cases heard before the committee of the other place. Third, we do not think that parliament is the place to be a rubber stamp for marital difficulties of people living in Quebec, in Newfoundland, or anywhere else. That is why we are taking the course of following in detail the evidence in each case. I hope that is a satisfactory answer.
One more question. Do you expect to discuss in detail each bill and to pass them?

At the rate we are going, one bill an hour, it would take us, on your count, 492 weeks, and I do not think we will be here this long. But if we return for another session and these bills are still before us, presumably over a course of 20 or 30 years we can touch on each one of them. The solution is very simple. We have the right honourable gentleman as the Prime Minister of this country. We have his cabinet, composed of his colleagues, astute, able and capable gentlemen that they are. Surely they can come up with an answer to this very vexing problem. We have offered them many solutions and alternatives. We even went so far as to pick the Prime Minister's greatest love, namely his love for royal commissions, and we asked him to appoint a royal commission on this question. This would satisfy our desires for the moment. So far the Prime Minister has decided to be as vacillating as he usually is, so we have no other course to follow but to proceed on each one. We shall have to go through each of these 492, plus 200 or 300 more added each year until this question is solved.
Now we have another witness. This is the key witness, the individual who knows about the night of June 13. This is the man who comes forward with the evidence about the pink pyjamas, ruffled beds, dented pillows, rumpled sheets, and all the other gory details which private investigators love to reveal to

the committee of the other place on the question of whether or not adultery has taken place. The other two witnesses, so far as the proof of adultery on June 13 is concerned, do not matter. One of them did not have the foggiest idea about that night, and the other one did not remember about that particular night. Now we have a Mr. Armand Masse, who gives his age as 22, his address as Montreal, and his occupation as a collector. He was sworn through an interpreter and I presume would have testified in the French language, and had his evidence interpreted all the way through by the interpreter attached to the committee in the other place. He was shown a picture of the respondent and is asked whether he recognized it, and he said it was the respondent. Then he is asked:
Did you have the opportunity to meet Mr.-
and then he gave the name of the respondent, to which he answered that he had, twice. Here is a gentleman who did not know the respondent, as the grocer did for seven years. He had not lived in the house as a boarder as the cutter, the other witness, had. He had met him on two occasions. Then the question is:
Could you tell us on these two occasions what happened?
A. The first time I went there I gave a reason for going there, and I asked him who was living there with him, in the apartment, and he showed me his boarder and his wife.
Mr. Chairman, can you put yourself in that position? A man comes to your house. He does not know you, meets you for the first time, gives you a reason for coming to you, and asks you who is living in your house. Would you automatically say: "Yes, here is my boarder and my wife", when this individual is just a collector, unless he represented himself as a private detective, or something like that? Then the next question is:
Is the person that he showed you as his wife present in this room?
A. Yes, there.
Then he pointed to somebody who the chairman discovered by question was the corespondent. This is a person, who is the corespondent, in the committee room according to two or three different witnesses, and it is a wonder to me that the lawyer did not take steps to give testimony with respect to the allegation of adultery inasmuch as she was there in the committee room. She did not have to give evidence. Perhaps her lawyer asked her and she said no, but it would have been much simpler than to have had this parade of witnesses, so far none of whom knew anything at all about the alleged adultery having taken place on the night of June 13. The chairman continued:
Do you know the petitioner sitting beside her counsel?

A. I haven't seen her before this morning.
Q. On the second occasion what happened?
This is the second time he went back to the house where the respondent lived.
A. I rang the bell about two o'clock in the morning. A lady came out on the balcony in her night attire and said she would call the police if we stayed there, so we went back.
I would point out that there is no further indication in the evidence as to who those persons were; whether this person Armand Masse, who classified himself as a collector, went back with somebody else, or what happened. But the word "we" is used. Then the lawyer asked further questions:
